source_text: Τὸν τοιοῦτον ἡδέως ἂν εἶδον καὶ δήμων καὶ γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης ἄρχοντα, καὶ πόλεων καὶ δήμων καὶ στρατοπέδων. Ὁ γὰρ τοῖς πάθεσι τῆς ψυχῆς τὸν λογισμὸν ἐπιστήσας, ῥᾳδίως ἂν ἐπισταίη καὶ ἀνθρώποις μετὰ τῶν θείων νόμων, ὥστε αὐτὸν ἐν πατρὸς τάξει τοῖς ἀρχομένοις εἶναι, μετὰ πάσης ἡμερότητος ὁμιλοῦντα ταῖς πόλεσιν. Ὁ δὲ ἀνθρώπων μὲν ἄρχειν δοκῶν, θυμῷ δὲ καὶ φιλαρχίᾳ καὶ ἡδοναῖς δουλεύων, πρῶτον μὲν καταγέλαστος εἶναι δό ξειεν ἂν τοῖς ἀρχομένοις, ὅτι στέφανον μὲν φορεῖ λιθοκόλλητον καὶ χρυσοῦν, σωφροσύνῃ δὲ οὐκ ἐστεφάνωται, καὶ ἁλουργίδι μὲν ὅλον τὸ σῶμα λάμπεται, τὴν δὲ ψυχὴν ἀκόσμητον ἔχει. Ἔπειτα δὲ οὐδὲ ὅπως μεταχειρίσαιτο τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπιστήσεται· ὁ γὰρ ἑαυτοῦ μὴ δυνηθεὶς ἄρχειν, πῶς ἂν ἑτέρους δυνηθείη κατευθύνειν τοῖς νόμοις; Εἰ δὲ βούλει καὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἑκατέρων ἰδεῖν, εὑρήσεις τὸν μὲν δαίμοσι μαχόμενον καὶ κρατοῦντα καὶ νικῶντα καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ στεφανούμενον· μετὰ γὰρ τῆς θείας ῥοπῆς ἐπὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἔρχεται, οὐρανίοις πεφραγμένος ὅπλοις, ὥστε ἀνάγκη τούτου γενέσθαι τὸ κράτος· τὸν δὲ βασιλέα βαρβάροις μαχόμενον. Ὅσῳ δὲ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ δαίμονες φοβερώτεροι, τοσούτῳ λαμπρότερος ὁ τούτων κρατῶν τοῦ νικῶντος ἐκείνους. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν ἑκατέρου πολέμου καταμαθεῖν βουληθείης, πολὺ τὸ οὐκ ἴσον εὑρήσεις. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὲρ εὐσεβείας καὶ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείας πολεμεῖ τοῖς δαίμοσιν, ἢ πόλεις ἢ κώμας ἐκ τῆς πλάνης ἐξαρπάσαι ποθῶν· ὁ δὲ μάχεται βαρβάροις ὑπὲρ τόπων ἢ ὅρων ἢ χρημάτων ἁρπασθέντων, ἢ πλεονεξίας καὶ ἔρωτος ἀρχῆς ἀδίκου παρακαλούσης ἐπὶ τὴν μάχην· ἔνθα δὴ πολλοὶ πολλάκις βασιλεῖς, τῶν μειζόνων ἐπιθυμήσαντες, καὶ τὰ παρόντα προσαπώλεσαν. Ἡ μὲν οὖν ἀρχὴ καὶ οἱ πόλεμοι τοσοῦτον ἀλλήλων διαφέροντας ἔδειξαν τόν τε βασιλέα, καὶ τὸν ἐσπουδακότα τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείᾳ συζῇν· γνοίη δ' ἄν τις αὐτοὺς ἀκριβῶς, τὸν βίον ἑκατέρου καὶ τὰς πράξεις τὰς παρ' ἡμέραν σκοπῶν. Εὕροι γὰρ ἂν ὡς ἀληθῶς τὸν μὲν ὁμιλοῦντα προφήταις, καὶ τῇ τοῦ Παύλου σοφίᾳ τὴν ψυχὴν καλλωπίζοντα, καὶ μεταπηδῶντα συνεχῶς ἀπὸ μὲν Μωσέως πρὸς Ἡσαΐαν, ἀπὸ δὲ τούτου πρὸς Ἰωάννην, ἀπὸ δὲ τούτου πρὸς ἕτερον· τὸν βασιλέα δὲ συνεχῶς ὁμιλοῦντα ταξιάρχοις καὶ ὑπάρχοις καὶ δορυφόροις· οἷς δέ τις ὁμιλεῖ συνεχῶς, τούτοις ἀφομοιοῦται τὸ ἦθος. Οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν μονάζων πρὸς τὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ προφητῶν ἤθη ἐκτυποῦται τὴν γνώμην, ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς πρὸς τὰ τῶν στρατηγῶν καὶ δορυφόρων καὶ ὑπασπιστῶν, ἀνθρώπων οἴνῳ δουλευόντων καὶ ἡδοναῖς χαριζομένων, καὶ τὸ πλέον τῆς ἡμέρας διατριβόντων ἐν πότῳ, οὐδὲν καίριον ἢ καλὸν διὰ τὸν οἶνον ἐπισταμένων. Οὕτως ἄρα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τὸν μονήρη βίον προσήκει μακαρίζειν μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν ἐν δυναστείᾳ καὶ βασιλείᾳ καὶ σκήπτροις. γʹ. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τῆς νυκτὸς τὸν χρόνον ἐξετάζειν βουληθείημεν, τὸν μοναχὸν μὲν ὀψόμεθα τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείᾳ καὶ ταῖς εὐχαῖς κοσμούμενον, πολὺ πρότερον ᾄδοντα τῶν ὀρνίθων, ἀγγέλοις συμβιοτεύοντα, Θεῷ συλλαλοῦντα, τῶν οὐρανίων ἀγαθῶν ἀπολαύοντα· τὸν δὲ πολλοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἐφεστηκότα καὶ δήμοις καὶ στρατοπέδοις, καὶ πολλῆς μὲν γῆς, πολλῆς δὲ ἄρχοντα θαλάττης, ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης ἀνατεταμένον καὶ ῥέγχοντα.
thought_title: The monk's true kingship and the king's shame
orientation: Chrysostom has just defined the true king as one who rules his passions, and now he compares how such a man would govern cities with how a passion-enslaved king actually behaves.
pass_a_gloss: Such a man I would gladly see ruling peoples and land and sea, and cities and peoples and armies. For the one who set his reason over the passions of the soul would easily stand over men too with the divine laws, so that he would be to his subjects in the rank of a father, conversing with the cities with all gentleness. But the one who seems to rule men, yet is enslaved to anger and love of power and pleasures, first would seem ridiculous to his subjects, because he wears a crown set with stones and golden, but is not crowned with self-control, and his whole body shines with purple, but he has his soul unadorned. Then he will not even know how to handle his rule; for the one who was not able to rule himself, how could he be able to guide others by the laws? And if you wish to see the war of each, you will find the one fighting demons and prevailing and conquering and being crowned by Christ; for with the divine inclination he comes to the war, fenced with heavenly weapons, so that of necessity the victory becomes his; and the king fighting barbarians. And by as much as demons are more fearful than men, by so much more splendid is the one who prevails over them than the one who conquers those. And if you should wish to learn the cause of each war, you will find much inequality. For the one fights the demons on behalf of devotion to God and the service of God, longing to snatch cities or villages out of error; but the other fights barbarians on behalf of places or borders or plundered money, or greed and desire for unjust rule urging him to the battle; where indeed many kings often, having desired greater things, lost also what they had. So then the rule and the wars showed the king and the one eager to live with the service of God differing from each other by so much; and one would know them precisely, examining the life of each and the daily deeds. For he would find truly the one conversing with prophets, and adorning his soul with the wisdom of Paul, and leaping continually from Moses to Isaiah, and from him to John, and from him to another; and the king continually conversing with commanders and governors and bodyguards; and with whom one converses continually, to these he is made like in character. Therefore the monk is stamped in his mind toward the characters of the apostles and prophets, but the king toward those of generals and bodyguards and shield-bearers, men enslaved to wine and gratifying pleasures, and spending the greater part of the day in drinking, knowing nothing timely or noble because of the wine. Thus then and for this reason it is fitting to bless the monastic life rather than the one in power and kingship and scepters. 3. And if we should wish to examine the time of night, we will see the monk adorned with the service of God and prayers, singing much earlier than the birds, living with angels, conversing with God, enjoying heavenly goods; and the one set over many nations and peoples and armies, and ruling much land and much sea, stretched out on the bed and snoring.

choices.why: The noun denotes the disordered desire for rule, parallel to θυμός and ἡδοναί as passions enslaving the king.
ῥοπή means the tipping of the scale or inclination; 'divine inclination' preserves the sense of God's decisive weight or favor in the monk's war.
The perfect participle of φράσσω means enclosed or fenced for protection; 'fenced with heavenly weapons' keeps the military image.
The compound ἐξαρπάζω means to seize and pull out; 'snatch out of error' conveys the rescue from deception.
The middle/passive of ἀφομοιόω means to become like or assimilate; the passive rendering keeps the sense that character is shaped by constant company.
ἐκτυπόω means to impress or stamp a form; 'is stamped in his mind' preserves the image of the monk's mind receiving the imprint of apostolic character.

pass_b_english: I would gladly see such a man ruling peoples and land and sea, and cities and nations and armies. For the one who has set his reason over the passions of his soul would easily stand over human beings as well, together with the laws of God, so that he would be in the place of a father to those under his rule, conversing with the cities with all gentleness. But the one who seems to rule human beings while he is enslaved to anger and love of power and pleasures—first, he would appear ridiculous to his subjects, because he wears a crown set with jewels and gold but is not crowned with self-control, and his whole body gleams with purple while his soul is unadorned. And then he will not even know how to manage his power. For the one who was not able to rule himself, how could he guide others straight by the laws?

And if you wish to see the war of each, you will find the one fighting against demons, and prevailing, and conquering, and being crowned by Christ. For he comes to the war with divine aid, fenced around with heavenly weapons, so that victory must necessarily be his. But the king fights against barbarians. And as much as demons are more terrifying than human beings, so much more brilliant is the one who prevails over them than the one who conquers those others. And if you should wish to understand the cause of each war, you will find a great inequality. For the one fights against demons for devotion to God and the service of God, longing to snatch cities or villages out of error. But the other fights against barbarians over places or borders or stolen money, or because greed and desire for unjust power call him to battle. There, indeed, many kings have often desired greater things and lost even what they already possessed.

So then, the power and the wars have shown the king and the one who is eager to live with the service of God to differ from each other by this much. And one would know them precisely by examining the life of each and their daily actions. For he would find, truly, the one conversing with prophets, adorning his soul with the wisdom of Paul, and leaping constantly from Moses to Isaiah, and from him to John, and from him to another. But the king constantly converses with commanders and governors and bodyguards. And the character of those with whom one constantly converses is the character one is made like. Therefore the monk's mind is stamped with the character of the apostles and prophets, but the king's with the character of generals and bodyguards and shield-bearers—men enslaved to wine and gratifying pleasures, who spend the greater part of the day in drinking, and know nothing timely or good because of the wine. So then, for this reason also it is fitting to call the monastic life happy rather than the life in power and kingship and scepters.

And if we should wish to examine the time of night as well, we will see the monk adorned with the service of God and with prayers, singing much earlier than the birds, living together with angels, conversing with God, enjoying the good things of heaven. But the one set over many nations and peoples and armies, ruling much land and much sea, is stretched out on his bed and snoring.

problems.why: ῥοπή means 'impetus/assistance/tilt of the scales', not 'inclination' as disposition; 'divine aid/assistance' is meant

problems.quote: lost what they already had in addition
problems.why: προσαπώλεσαν means 'lost in addition' or 'lost as well', but 'what they already had in addition' is unclear; 'lost what they had as well' or 'lost even what they possessed'
problems.fix: lost even what they already possessed
problems.ruling: 'what they already had in addition' is awkward/misleading; προσαπώλεσαν = 'lost even what they had' (τὰ παρόντα).

edits.old: lost what they already had in addition
edits.new: lost even what they already possessed

fixed: Changed 'with the divine inclination' to 'with divine aid' because ῥοπή here means assistance or tilt of the scales, not disposition.
Changed 'lost what they already had in addition' to 'lost even what they already possessed' because προσαπώλεσαν means lost in addition, and the original phrasing was unclear.

last_rejected.quote: the one who has set his reason over the passions of his soul
last_rejected.source_quote: Ὁ γὰρ τοῖς πάθεσι τῆς ψυχῆς τὸν λογισμὸν ἐπιστήσας
last_rejected.why: ἐπιστήσας means 'set over/appointed as commander,' not passive 'has set'; agency and force weakened.
last_rejected.fix: For the one who has appointed reason as commander over the passions of his soul
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπιστήσας is active aorist 'having set/placed'; 'has set over' captures agency correctly.

last_rejected.quote: would easily stand over human beings as well, together with the laws of God
last_rejected.source_quote: ῥᾳδίως ἂν ἐπισταίη καὶ ἀνθρώποις μετὰ τῶν θείων νόμων
last_rejected.why: ἐπισταίη means 'rule/command,' not 'stand over'; 'with' not 'together with' the laws.
last_rejected.fix: would easily rule human beings as well, with the divine laws
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπισταίη means 'be in charge/rule'; 'stand over' is acceptable; μετὰ + gen. = 'with' laws.

last_rejected.quote: conversing with the cities with all gentleness
last_rejected.why: ὁμιλοῦντα is middle voice, 'associating/dealing with,' not active 'conversing with' cities as interlocutors.
last_rejected.fix: dealing with cities with all gentleness
last_rejected.ruling: ὁμιλεῖν means 'associate/converse/deal with'; 'conversing with cities' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: he will not even know how to manage his power
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐδὲ ὅπως μεταχειρίσαιτο τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπιστήσεται
last_rejected.why: ἐπιστήσεται is future of ἐπίσταμαι 'know,' but ὅπως with optative shows he won't understand how to manage rule.
last_rejected.fix: he will not even understand how to manage his rule
last_rejected.ruling: Translation correctly conveys 'will not know how to manage his rule'; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: For he comes to the war with divine aid
last_rejected.source_quote: μετὰ γὰρ τῆς θείας ῥοπῆς ἐπὶ τὸν πόλεμον ἔρχεται
last_rejected.why: ῥοπῆς means 'inclination/weight/momentum,' not 'aid'; 'divine inclination/assistance' is specific sense.
last_rejected.fix: For with divine inclination he comes to the war
last_rejected.ruling: ῥοπή can mean 'weight/influence/aid'; 'divine aid' is reasonable contextual rendering.

last_rejected.why: πεφραγμένος is perfect passive participle 'having been fenced,' but 'armed/equipped' better captures sense.
last_rejected.ruling: πεφραγμένος = 'fenced/protected'; 'fenced around with weapons' is acceptable metaphorical rendering.

last_rejected.quote: the one who prevails over them than the one who conquers those others
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ τούτων κρατῶν τοῦ νικῶντος ἐκείνους
last_rejected.why: κρατῶν means 'masters/conquers,' νικῶντος means 'conquering'; both are conquering, but κρατῶν is stronger 'mastering.'
last_rejected.fix: the one who masters them than the one who conquers those others
last_rejected.ruling: κρατῶν and νικῶντος overlap in meaning; 'prevails/conquers' distinction is adequate.

last_rejected.quote: the one who is eager to live with the service of God
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸν ἐσπουδακότα τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείᾳ συζῇν
last_rejected.why: συζῇν means 'live together with/associate with,' not 'live with' in sense of lifestyle; 'devoted to living in company with God's service.'
last_rejected.fix: the one eager to live in fellowship with the service of God
last_rejected.ruling: συζῇν τῇ λατρείᾳ = 'live with/in company with God's service'; 'live with' is acceptable.

last_rejected.quote: the monk's mind is stamped with the character
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ μὲν μονάζων πρὸς τὰ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ προφητῶν ἤθη ἐκτυποῦται τὴν γνώμην
last_rejected.why: ἐκτυποῦται τὴν γνώμην means 'his mind is molded,' but πρὸς τὰ ἤθη shows 'after the pattern of' not 'with the character of.'
last_rejected.fix: the monk's mind is molded after the ways of the apostles and prophets
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκτυποῦται τὴν γνώμην πρὸς τὰ ἤθη = 'mind molded after the character'; 'stamped with character' is adequate.

last_rejected.quote: men enslaved to wine and gratifying pleasures
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀνθρώπων οἴνῳ δουλευόντων καὶ ἡδοναῖς χαριζομένων
last_rejected.why: χαριζομένων means 'indulging/pleasing' pleasures, not 'gratifying' as transitive; 'devoted to pleasures.'
last_rejected.fix: men enslaved to wine and devoted to pleasures
last_rejected.ruling: χαριζομένων ἡδοναῖς = 'gratifying/indulging pleasures'; 'gratifying' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: know nothing timely or good because of the wine
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐδὲν καίριον ἢ καλὸν διὰ τὸν οἶνον ἐπισταμένων
last_rejected.why: ἐπισταμένων means 'knowing/understanding,' but καίριον means 'seasonable/opportune/decisive,' not 'timely' in modern sense.
last_rejected.fix: knowing nothing opportune or excellent because of the wine
last_rejected.ruling: καίριον = 'timely/opportune'; 'timely' is standard rendering, no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: it is fitting to call the monastic life happy
last_rejected.why: μακαρίζειν means 'count blessed/praise as happy,' stronger than 'call happy'; 'hold blessed' or 'account blessed.'
last_rejected.fix: it is fitting to count the monastic life blessed
last_rejected.ruling: μακαρίζειν = 'call/count blessed/happy'; 'call happy' is within normal range.
